speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In answer to my hon. friend for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) I may say that the rights of the federal government and the provinces, as respects many important subjects, are determined by the British North America Act. The matter of property and civil rights, according to that act, is assigned to the provinces. The provinces have all along claimed, and I think rightly, that under that provision factory legislation, matters of employment, questions relating to master and servant and the like, come within their jurisdiction and not within the jurisdiction of the federal government. Such, in my opinion, is a sound and proper interpretation of that section of the act. if dealing with employment is part of the duty of the provinces, action regarding unemployment would also seem to fall within the same category. The view this government has taken has been that any such relief granted by it in the past has been by reason of a national emergency arising out of the war. Such aid was not given because of an obligation imposed upon the federal government by the British North America Act; it was to meet an emergency national in its character. Now the time has come when it is necessary to draw the line. I want to point out to my hon. friend-and I think it is well worth pointing out to hon. gentlemen as a whole-that during the period of the war the debt of the federal government was increased enormously; some two billions of dollars were added to the national debt, and this government has now to ask parliament for an appropriation of 8140,000,000 to meet the interest on that debt alone. On the other hand the provinces, during the period of the war, added virtually nothing to their public debt as a consequence of that great struggle; the whole burden fell on the federal treasuiy which is now having difficulty in raising the money needed for the purposes of the nation. Moreover the provinces, or some of them at least, are beginning to have surpluses instead of deficits, and we feel, and I think the House will agree, that if this government is to be expected to carry out the obligations that clearly fall upon it we ought to tell the provinces that where they can reasonably find the means of dealing with those matters that come within their particular jurisdiction they should make an effort to do so.

The Prime Minister has furnished the information which I sought to get in my questions to the minister, namely, that the question of unemployment is pri-' manly one that rests upon the provincial governments and that it is only under unusual conditions, such, for example, as those which ariSe out of war, that the federal government has any responsibility. So that we ma; assume from the statements of the Prime Minister and the minister that henceforth the attitude of the federal government on the question of unemployment will be a negative one excepting in cases of national emergency arising out .of war

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: National emergency of any kind.

I cannot conceive that there would be any other national emergency except such as stated, and therefore action on the part of the federal parliament would be confined to what I might call a war emergency. I get letters all the time from people saying, "Why don't you get after the government, they are not doing anything for unemployment?" I frankly confess that I agree with the attitude assumed by the government -that this is a provincial problem, not a federal problem; and the sooner the public learn where they stand the quicker they will be able to seek and enforce a remedy. I am therefore glad the Prime Minister has made this statement because it tends to make clear something which has been shrouded in mystery in the past. I presume that henceforth-excepting as regards situations growing out of war-we may conclude that the federal government has finished with the question of unemployment.

I appreciate the position of the federal government with regard to unemployment, and I am certainly glad that the Prime Minister has given us this explanation. We shall now, as provinces and municipalities, know that there is very little hope of expecting anything in the way of relief from the Dominion government except in extreme cases. However, I would like just to add this: While the Prime Minister has no doubt given us the proper interpretation of the act, nevertheless I would submit it is not a satisfactory one. If the act has been correctly interpreted by the Prime Minister I think it will have to be changed. For surely it is not fair that the Dominion government-possessing the power by its fiscal policy pretty well to regulate the industrial life of the country, and the power also by its immigration policies to flood this

Supply-Labour
country with labour that cannot be employed -should pass on the unemployment burden to the provincial and municipal authorities. I would suggest that if this course is going to be continued the provinces be granted the right to map out their own tariff and immigration policies so as to be able to meet the emergency confronting them.

I want to ask the minister a question in connection with a statement he made in answer to the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) about the refusal of his department, if such it be, to pay to the city of Calgary the sum of approximately 81,800 because, as he suggests, no proper body has been constituted in accordance with the provisions of Privy Council Order No. 220. I do not know what the terms of this order in council are, but I do know that the city of Calgary has a regularly constituted and responsible organization to deal with the matter of unemployment, and that there is a responsible official in charge of the office. Returned soldiers have received relief during the past winter to the amount of something over 85,000, and acting and relying on the previous attitude of the government, and the former governments, the city of Calgary had a right to expect that approximately 81,800 of that amount would be borne by the federal government. If a mere technicality stands in the way surely the minister is not going to take advantage of it in order to deprive the city of Calgary of this not inconsiderable amount which has been expended for the relief of returned soldiers. I would therefore like to know from the minister what limitations stand in the way of carrying out my suggestion and if the department proposes to rely upon those limitations or whether, regardless of non-compliance with the terms of the order in council referred to, an adequate amount will be placed in the Supplementary Estimates to cover this item.

I will read Privy Council Order No. 220 to the committee, and then ask my hon. friend to suggest whether, in his judgment, the Minister of Labour-who is subject to criticism when he does not do things according to instructions-is permitted to recognize any bills of the kind presented by the city of Calgary.
Is there any dispute as to whether or not the city of Qalgary has properly expended this sum for unemployment?

No, none whatever. The city of Calgary, in an orderly way and in due
course, as it was necessary, and as the bills were presented, paid the amount without any federal grant, and thereby obviated the necessity of the Dominion government in any way, under order in council 220, coming to their assistance. This order No. 220 was not issued for the purpose of coming to the assistance of any municipality that accepted, dealt with and paid bills of the kind, but I still would like to read the order in council to my hon. friend as the point has been raised, and then ask him for his own version of it. The order in council reads:
The committeethe Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 30th January, 1923, from the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, submitting that, while employment conditions generally have improved since the winter of 1921-22, unemployment still exists, particularly in the larger centres of population, to an extent necessitating the provision of relief by municipalities and charitable organizations.
The minister states that representations have been received indicating that certain of those reduced to a condition of distress in consequence of unemployment are former members of the Forces, including some suffering from disabilities which, although not attributable to war service, and therefore not pensionable, place the men concerned in most cases under a handicap in competing in the general labour market; such men not being, however, eligible to receive assistance extended by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment to men whose disabilities are attributable to their services with the Forces during the war.
Previous federal regulations with respect to federal co-operation with local authorities in the relief of un-ployment have properly emphasized the principle that the matter of caring for unemployed persons is fundamentally a responsibility of the local authorities, and that the federal authorities are justified in undertaking any share of the obligation arising only under abnormal conditions. It is, however, submitted that the situation above indicated is one which justified and requires federal action by way of co-operation in the relief of unemployed ex-service men of the class described.
Information received shows that in certain municipalities central bodies, composed of representatives of the municipality and of the various charitable and veteran organizations, have been formed for the administration of relief to ex-service men unable to procure work and in necessitous circumstances, and such organizations are regarded as serving excellent purpose.
The minister accordingly recommends that where any organization composed as above, has, since January 1st, 1923, made disbursements in relief of the necessities of ex-service men of the class indicated in paragraph 2 as above, the federal authorities will reimburse such relief bodies to the extent of one-third of such disbursements incurred since that date; provided that no grant shall be payable by the federal authorities save when the accounts submitted for payment have been approved by the Minister of Labour and Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment; the grants in question to be paid, the Minister of Labour concurring, from the appropriation for the relief of unemployment for the present fiscal year and administered under the authority of the Minister of Labour.
And it is duly signed. Therefore I call the attention of my hon. friend from Calgarv to the fact that the 81,800 that he is interested in securing for the city of Calgary was paid by the municipality through its
Supply-Labour

relief department alone, and without any consideration or recognition of this order in council, and it is only proper to say that I do not think that, by any stretch of imagination, sympathetic or otherwise, I could indicate that under this order in council the city of Calgary qualifies to be reimbursed the $1,800.

The minister must certainly realize that, while the letter of the law has not perhaps been complied with the spirit of the law has been. Is it not possible for him, under those circumstances, to put in the supplementary estimates an amount sufficient to cover this particulaf item?

Would my hon. friend be surprised to know that if I said yes, which I have no right to do, it would mean the presentation of bills very much greater in amount from various places from which we have not heard one word so far. Where It means $1,800 in the case of Calgary, I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that, in different parts of Canada, several thousand dollars would be claimed in the same way, although the money had been paid out in the ordinary course of business, and had been regarded having been properly paid by the relief departments of the various municipalities.

I would like to point out that there is a slight difference between the case of Calgary and that of any other supposed case to which the minister has alluded. For instance, I inquired from the Minister of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment for his interpretation of this particular order in council . which the Minister of Labour has just read, and according to the interpretation given me by the minister of the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment, the federal government was liable for one-third of the amount of money expended by the relief board of Calgary.' I communicated this information to Mr. H. B. Adshead, who is the administrator of the department of municipal service in Calgary. That statement was published in the public press and the people of Calgary had been relying on the government to recoup them that amount of money. So that there is a slight difference between this case and any supposed case that might come before the minister. Therefore I would urge the Minister of Labour to consider the appeal of Calgary in this regard, set aside what, after all, is only a technicality and grant this request.

Some time ago I asked the minister a question relative to the statistics of the department. I find, besides the names that I have mentioned, that there are 20

clerks in this department interested in the compilation of statistics. It seems to me that the minister can use the pooling method to great advantage there.

Although a number of statistical clerks were transferred to the regular statistical department, it is still necessary, and has been held so, even by the chief of the Bureau of Statistics to have in the Labour department a considerable number of employees especially qualified to look after the compilation of labour statistics. It is for that purpose that a Statistical branch is still being maintained in the Labour department, and in that branch th6re are sixteen employees altogether.

I can count twenty. If
the minister will look down the list, he will find one chief statistician, one head statistical clerk, three principal statistical clerks, a little further down he will find six senior statistical clerks. My hon. friend is quite right. There is the Statistical branch for the purpose of compiling labour organization figures and matters in connection with that. Thus, there are two branches of the Labour department, a Statistical branch and an Employment Service branch, in which there are a number of statistical clerks, compiling and handling figures that we could not get, I understand, through the regular statistical department of the government under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
What are the special matters referring to labour for which these statistics are being compiled?

Hours of employment,
wage rates, cost of living in its various classifications, rentals which have an important bearing on the cost of living and all such items as that. These are all matters that it has been regarded as necessary to maintain as reasonably as possible accurate figures on.

I have the occupations of the various annuitants, covering 176 occupations, and then certain other information in answer to questions asked the other night, but I have not the information for which my hon. friend now asks. The minister says
that one feature of the statistics that are being compiled relates to the cost of living. I would infer from the discussion that took place a few nights ago that a good deal of the information is sent in from those who are paid a very small sum in outlying districts. During the war, I believe, it was required of those handling meat and produce of all kinds to file a monthly statement with the department regarding the prices at which these commodities were being sold. Is this practice still in vogue, or has this matter been turned over to the Bureau of Statistics?

The duties of the statistical branch relate, first, to prices and the cost of living; secondly, to wages and hours of labour, including industrial agreements; and thirdly, to strikes and lockouts. With regard to the first, there is published, monthly, information concerning retail and wholesale prices in Canada and other countries; and so far as wages and hours of labour are concerned, there appears monthly in the Labour Gazette a summary analysis of recent industrial agreements, schedules of wages, and so forth; and information is also given as to strikes and lockouts.
Is that a Labour department form that my hon. friend is referring to?
It is from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.

That has nothing to do with my department, although I believe that some information of the kind goes to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I do not think that information is collected by the Department of Labour, but we probably get from the Bureau of Statistics an analysis of the results that may be secured through this questionnaire.
The information sent out through the Labour Gazette is compiled from the statistics arrived at in this way.
The department maintains also some 60 or more correspondents to check up on the figures obtained in the various towns.

I see by the statistics which the Professor of Economics of McMas-ter University has been compiling for some years, that the cost of living has been rising for several months now. Is that the same verdict as the officers of the department find?

He is yet quite as interested.

He does not know what the results of his own department are as to the cost of living. I was asking whether the department's figures agreed in tendency with those of the Professor of Economics of Mc-Master University showing an increase in the cost of living.
The figures did show a slight seasonal rise as we have found in all winters in Canada in the past.
What is the minister going to do to bring the cost down? He has been failing in all his pledges in that regard.
We are working nicely in that direction if you will keep out of the road.
The minister is working all right, but the results are exactly the opposite of what he is working for.
We are doing nicely, thank you.

I know that the minister is drawing his salary, but the cost of living keeps going up. The minister made terrible strictures on the late government, and promised to devote his tremendous abilities to the reduction of the cost of living. That was to be his ambition in public life. That was what he set his heart upon; he was going to relieve the poor.
Some job.

Some job! Yes, now that my hon. friend is in the department he finds that it is "some job." The cost of living, which went down 24 points in the official scale in 1921 from what it was 12 months before, is now higher than it was when the minister took office. It is going the wrong way. Does the minister not think it is time for him to give place to somebody else?
I suggest that my right hon. friend read Babson instead of the pessimists that he has been reading.

I am not criticizing Babson at all-I have been reading the hon. minister. He should judge his conduct by his own standard. I am asking him in what state of mind is he now, having not. only failed to carry on the good work instituted by
